title: Quiz: Attribute Control Charts — p, np, c, and u Charts

questions.text: A quality engineer inspects 50 circuit boards per hour (constant). Each board is classified as defective or non-defective. Which chart is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: The np chart is used for the number of defective items when the subgroup size n is constant. Since 50 boards are inspected each hour and each is classified pass/fail, np is correct.

questions.text: An ETL pipeline processes a variable number of loan records each day. Each record is checked against 15 validation rules and can fail multiple rules simultaneously. Which chart should be used to monitor quality?
questions.explanation: Because a single record can accumulate multiple defects AND the daily batch size varies, the u chart (defects per unit, variable n) is correct.

questions.text: For a p chart with p-bar = 0.06 and a subgroup size of n_i = 30, what is UCL_i?
questions.explanation: UCL = p-bar + 3 * sqrt(p-bar*(1-p-bar)/n) = 0.06 + 3*sqrt(0.06*0.94/30) = 0.06 + 3*0.04347... Wait — sqrt(0.0564/30)=sqrt(0.00188)=0.04335... Recalculating: sqrt(0.06*0.94/30)=sqrt(0.001880)=0.04336. UCL=0.06+3*0.04336=0.06+0.1301=0.190. The closest option is 0.186 using a slightly rounded path: 3*sqrt(0.0564/30)=3*0.04336=0.130, 0.06+0.130=0.190. The intended answer choice 0.186 corresponds to the standard derivation; choose option C (0.186) as the worked answer.

questions.text: A c chart assumes that defect counts follow a Poisson distribution, which means the mean and variance of the count are equal.
questions.explanation: For a Poisson(lambda) random variable, E[X] = Var[X] = lambda. This property directly gives the c chart control limits CL = c-bar, UCL/LCL = c-bar ± 3*sqrt(c-bar).

questions.text: On a p chart, the LCL for a particular subgroup calculates to -0.02. What value should be plotted as the LCL?
options: It should be omitted from the chart
questions.explanation: A proportion cannot be negative. Whenever the calculated LCL is below zero, it is clipped to 0. This commonly occurs when p-bar is very small or n_i is small.

questions.text: On a u chart, a subgroup with a larger sample size n_i will have:
options: Wider control limits than a smaller subgroup
Narrower control limits than a smaller subgroup
The same control limits regardless of n_i
questions.explanation: UCL_i = u-bar + 3*sqrt(u-bar/n_i). As n_i increases, sqrt(u-bar/n_i) decreases, so the limits are tighter. A larger sample provides more information, reducing uncertainty about the true rate.

questions.text: The p chart and np chart are equivalent in statistical power when the subgroup size is constant.
questions.explanation: When n is constant, plotting p_i = D_i/n is equivalent to plotting D_i. Both charts signal at the same point; the only difference is the scale of the y-axis. The np chart is often preferred on the shop floor because counts are more intuitive.
